keySentence: The lost boys followed Peter because he made them feel brave and free.

facts.Page story text 1 (draft, teacher check: The lost boys had every reason to be frightened living in Neverland each and every dangerous day. Hook's pirates were always lurking nearby and the island had real dangers around every single corner. But when Peter was leading them none of those dangers felt as large as they actually and truly were. He ran toward trouble with a crow of pure joy that made the boys want to run right there beside him. He told them constantly that they were the fiercest and the freest children anywhere in the whole world. Under his leadership even the most timid and uncertain boy found himself doing things he had thought impossible. The lost boys followed Peter because he made them feel brave and free.
facts.Page story text 2 (draft, teacher check: The most important thing Peter Pan gave the lost boys was not shelter or food or protection from the pirates. It was the experience of feeling genuinely brave and completely free on a consistent and reliable daily basis. Before Peter they had each felt small and lost and uncertain in a world that was much larger than they were. Peter reorganized their self-understanding completely without ever lecturing them or explaining what he was doing. He simply treated them as brave and free until the treatment became the truth and the truth became permanent. The boys who had once hidden from shadows were now charging onto pirate ships with swords drawn and crowing. This was not performance — it was the actual emergence of qualities that had been waiting inside each of them. The lost boys followed Peter because he made them feel brave and free.
facts.Page story text 3 (draft, teacher check: The transformation of the lost boys under Peter Pan's leadership raises a profound question about human potential. Were the boys always capable of the bravery they displayed, or did Peter somehow create that bravery in them? The answer seems to be neither quite right and both partly right simultaneously, which makes the question interesting. The potential was there — but potential unrealized and unrecognized is functionally the same as potential absent. Peter's specific contribution was not the creation of courage but the removal of the obstacles that concealed it. Those obstacles were primarily internal — beliefs about what they were and weren't capable of and worthy of being. By replacing those beliefs with his own radical confidence in them, Peter liberated what had always been available. The greatest leaders do not make people into something they weren't — they reveal people to themselves for the first time. The lost boys followed Peter because he made them feel brave and free.
